name: Men's makeup (contour, bronzer, highlight)

card.summary: Subtle shading and highlighting aimed at sharpening the jaw and cheekbones; documented in makeup practice but unstudied for male attractiveness.
card.note: No clinical studies on effects of male contouring on perceived attractiveness were found.

lead: Men's contour, bronzer and highlight use shading and light to make the face look more defined. A shade one or two tones darker than the skin goes into the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create shadow and a slimmer, more sculpted look, while a lighter shade goes on prominent areas such as the cheek apples, nose tip and T-zone.[1] Bronzer adds warmth and depth to the skin overall. In looksmaxxing terms, the aim is a sharper jaw, higher-looking cheekbones and a straighter nose, achieved in minutes and washed off at the end of the day.[4]

The technique comes from theatre and film. Elizabethan stage actors used chalk and soot so audiences could read their faces, Max Factor Sr. added shading so faces would not look flat on camera and presented a contouring tutorial for different face shapes in 1945, and Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward introduced sculpting to the general public.[1][5] Celebrity use and dedicated contour and strobing products made it mainstream in the 2010s.[1]

Male cosmetics have a long history, from eye pigments in ancient Egypt to powdered skin in Elizabethan England, but were a niche market until the late 1990s.[2] Since then, male beauty creators on YouTube, retail launches aimed at men and survey data on younger consumers have pushed men's makeup toward the mainstream.[2][7] No published study has examined how contouring changes the perceived attractiveness of men.

angle.text: Shading and highlighting change how light falls on the face, so the jaw, cheekbones and nose can look more defined straight away. Practitioners use it for photos, video and events, and as a reversible way to try a sharper look.

infobox: Powder or cream contour palettes, highlighters, bronzer[1]

paras: Contouring places warm or cool darker shades in the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create a slimming, sculpted look. Highlighting uses lighter shades on the cheek apples, nose tip and T-zone, and strobing relies mainly on light shades with little or no darker shading.[1] Powder contour products are often sold as palettes with both light and dark shades, while cream products give a more emphasized look.[1]

Wikipedia describes contouring as a way to accentuate existing features or hide and change unwanted ones, and notes that drag performers use it to emphasize feminine features and soften masculine ones.[1] Bronzer is not covered in that article; it is generally used to add warmth to the skin and to shade the face's outer edges.

sections.h: How it is meant to help appearance
paras: The features people try to emphasise with male contouring correspond to traits discussed in attractiveness research. Wikipedia's article on facial attractiveness reports that angular male jawlines are favoured in Western countries, that men with low submental fat are rated as having better jawlines, and that some studies found a preference for high cheekbones, while also noting that preferences vary by population.[8] Shading under the jaw and in the cheek hollows is intended to mimic those contours optically, and highlighter is intended to lift the cheekbone and brow area.[1][4]
Because the effect is optical, it depends on lighting and camera angle; practitioners use it mainly for photos, video and events and as a reversible way to try a different look.[4]

Elizabethan stage actors used chalk and soot so audiences could read their expressions. When electric stage lighting made soot impractical in the late 1800s, greasepaint replaced it. In the 1920s and 1930s Marlene Dietrich shaded her face to emphasise its lines for film, and in 1934 Max Factor Sr. added shading so faces would not look flat on camera; in 1945 he presented a contouring tutorial for different face shapes.[1] Factor, born Maksymilian Faktorowicz in Poland, moved to Los Angeles in 1904 and by 1914 had developed a flexible greasepaint suited to film, and his company launched a Panchromatic line in 1929 for the new film stocks.[6]

The 1950s saw stars such as Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor wear subtle contouring.[1] Makeup artist Kevyn Aucoin (1962 to 2002), who worked for Vogue and with many celebrities, wrote The Art of Makeup (1994), Making Faces (1997) and Face Forward (2000); Wikipedia says Face Forward was widely noted for introducing sculpting and contouring to the general public, since the technique had previously been used mainly in drag and stage makeup.[5] In the 2010s Kim Kardashian and other celebrities popularised it, beauty brands began producing contour and strobing products, and in 2017 the New York Times called it a golden age of contouring.[1]

Wikipedia records men's cosmetic use across cultures, including dark eye pigments in ancient Egypt, powdered skin in Elizabethan England and the white base used by male kabuki actors. Roman society frowned on male cosmetic use. Men's beauty products were scarce until the late 1990s.[2]

According to the same article, some men use concealer to cover acne marks and freckles and some use cosmetics to enhance their appearance, while older men use products to even out skin tone and reduce visible wrinkles and age spots.[2] It reports that only about 17 percent of men consider makeup important in daily life, though 97 percent use skincare, and that men's packaging tends to use simpler, darker colours to reduce resistance to cosmetics.[2]

Wikipedia names US beauty YouTubers Patrick Starr and James Charles among prominent male creators, reports that French influencer Bach Buquen became popular in 2024 for applying makeup in public, and notes Chinese streamer Li Jiaqi selling 15,000 lipsticks in five minutes on 11 November 2018.[2] A CNBC report published on 14 January 2026 dates the modern men's makeup movement to CoverGirl naming 17-year-old James Charles its first CoverBoy in 2016.[7]

The same report cites Mintel data that 68 percent of US Gen Z men aged 18 to 27 used facial skincare in 2024, up from 42 percent two years earlier, Statista data that the share of US men who never wear makeup fell from over 90 percent in 2019 to about 75 percent in 2024, and an Ipsos survey in which about 15 percent of US heterosexual men aged 18 to 65 used cosmetics in 2022 with another 17 percent willing to consider it.[7] Brands it lists include War Paint, Stryx and Haus Labs, a Target launch of the men-focused line TONE in July 2025, and Papatui, launched by Dwayne Johnson at Target in 2024.[7]

Men quoted in that coverage describe makeup as maintenance rather than vanity, citing concealer or tinted moisturiser to look less tired, brow gel, and tinted SPF, and routines that begin with skincare and expand.[7] Contouring and bronzer are mentioned in some coverage as personal choices alongside concealing blemishes, though that mainstream reporting centres on subtler products.[7]

Looksmax.org has threads on using bronzer and contour to change the apparent shape of the face, with users presenting them as a low-cost, non-permanent way to simulate stronger bone structure; one thread is titled for the claim that bronzer, contour and fake tan can change nearly the whole face.[4] Another asks whether cheek-hollow contour lines should be curved or straight, and runs a poll on it.[9] Supporters treat makeup as one of the style-oriented tools alongside grooming and hair, since the effect is optical and can be matched to lighting and camera angle. Others in the community regard makeup as outside the practice or prefer permanent changes such as fat loss or surgery.

Related approaches in the same area include self-tanning and bronzing for skin tone, concealer and tinted moisturiser for blemishes, brow grooming and gel, and non-makeup routes to a sharper jaw and cheeks such as body-fat reduction. Lighting and camera position are discussed in the same threads as ways to change how contours read in photographs.[4]
No studies found. Published literature on male cosmetic contouring concerns surgical and device-based body contouring, which is a different subject.

lore.intro: Male contouring appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a cheap, reversible way to simulate stronger bone structure.[4]

claims.claim: Contour and bronzer can change the apparent shape of the whole face.
claims.believers: Proponents say shading creates the appearance of sharper structure at low cost and with no permanence.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes contouring as using shading to define and sculpt facial structure.[1] No studies were found on how it changes perceived male attractiveness.

claims.claim: Makeup carries stigma for men that limits its use.
claims.believers: Users report hesitancy because of social expectations.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states male cosmetics are not as widely accepted as female cosmetics, and CNBC reporting describes the share of US men who never wear makeup falling from over 90 percent in 2019 to about 75 percent in 2024.[2][7]

claims.claim: Shading under the jaw and in the cheek hollows mimics a sharper bone structure.
claims.believers: Forum users describe jaw and cheek contour as a way to look as if they had more defined bone structure.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that angular jawlines and low submental fat are favoured in Western settings and that some studies found a preference for high cheekbones; it describes no trials of contouring itself.[1][8]

claims.claim: Makeup works best in photos and under controlled lighting.
claims.believers: Users say the effect depends on lighting and camera angle, which can be matched to the shading.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's history credits film shading with preventing flat-looking faces on camera.[1]

claims.claim: Subtle products such as concealer and tinted moisturiser are the main male use.
claims.believers: Men quoted in news coverage describe makeup as maintenance, used to look less tired or cover acne.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports men use cosmetics to cover flaws such as acne marks and freckles or to enhance appearance.[2]

claims.claim: Makeup is a temporary stand-in for permanent changes such as fat loss or surgery.
claims.believers: Some members prefer permanent changes and treat makeup as a stopgap or as outside the practice.
claims.experts: No studies compare cosmetic shading with permanent approaches for male facial appearance.
